newsitem.title: CHINA: China drafts rules for lawyers, probes ethics.
newsitem.headline: China drafts rules for lawyers, probes ethics.

text.p: China is drafting regulations to tighten control of its lawyers and law firms and has launched a nationwide inspection of their professional ethics, the China Daily said on Thursday.

The rules were intended to standardise professional performance, lawyer-client relations and the administration of lawyers. It would go into effect along with the nation's first Lawyer's Law on January 1, 1997, the newspaper said.
"The Ministry of Justice's move to tighten control of lawyers and law firms is aimed at enhancing professional conduct and standardising legal services," it said.
The ministry was half-way through a two-month nationwide examination of lawyer's professional ethics, under which offenders would face disciplinary action, it said.

Most Chinese lawyers were well qualified, but problems such as unscrupulous billing, unfair and competitive practices and even illegal conduct continued to trouble the profession, China Daily quoted Vice-Minister of Justice Zhang Geng as saying.
In recent years, Beijing has been working to create a cohesive body of law to end decades of government through a confusion of decrees, laws and regulations.
Opportunities for lawyers would increase as civil suits became more common and the legal system adopted a more adversarial approach, China Daily said.
China now had 95,000 lawyers and 7,200 law firms, of which 5,500 were state-funded, 500 cooperatives and 1,200 partnerships, it added.
New registration regulations stipulate that law firms have assets worth more than 100,000 yuan ($12,000) and at least three lawyers, the Xinhua news agency said in a separate report.
State-funded law firms were set up by judicial departments, and no institutions or individuals would be allowed to interfere in their financial affairs or legal practice, it said.
